title: Old age as a messenger
hook: a first gray hair in the bathroom mirror, and a king who asked his barber to watch for it
tomorrow: an old monk is told he can ease up. what does he say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's body as an old cart, held together with straps and still on the road. The old cart. Today, the quiet moment a body first sends word that it's ageing.

A first gray hair turns up in the mirror, and the reflex is to pluck it, dye it, or laugh it off. A sutta tells of King Makhadeva, who did something stranger. He asked his barber: when you see gray hairs on my head, tell me. Years later, the barber did. The king had the gray hair plucked and laid in his palm, and he looked at it. What do you do with news like that? Here's his answer, and an old psalm's answer beside it.
screen: `A FIRST GRAY HAIR.` → `TELL ME WHEN YOU SEE IT.` → `A GRAY HAIR IN HIS PALM.`

segments.voice: The king gives the barber a village as a reward for the news. Then he calls his eldest son and says: the messengers of the gods have appeared; gray hairs are seen on my head. He hands over the kingdom and goes forth to practice, asking his son to keep the custom and pass it on. Elsewhere the Buddha names these messengers: an old person, a sick person, a dead person, each one sent to wake us up. So the gray hair isn't bad news. It's a messenger, and its message is: what matters, while there's time? Now a neighbor who heard a messenger too. A psalm in the Hebrew Bible, prayed by Jews and Christians, asks: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Shared: both see the passing of days as a teacher. Neither treats age as only loss; both turn it toward wisdom and the heart. Different, and honestly so: the psalm is a prayer, asking God to teach the counting. In the sutta, nobody is asked; the gray hair is the messenger, and the king answers by going forth himself. Two old texts, two ways of listening, one gray hair in the palm. And the custom, the sutta says, was meant to be passed down, from father to son.
screen: `A VILLAGE FOR THE BARBER.` · `THE MESSENGERS HAVE APPEARED.` · `A NEIGHBOR: NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · `SHARED, AND HONESTLY DIFFERENT.` · then, large: `THE MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: Look at the back of one hand, slowly, for the whole sit: the lines, the veins, a scar, the knuckles. Look at it the way the king looked at the hair in his palm, without judging, as something that has worked hard for you. Let whatever it says about time be a message, received kindly.
Old age as a messenger: a gray hair, a slower step, read not as bad news but as a reminder of what matters.
screen: `OLD AGE AS A MESSENGER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: the messenger, welcomed, not chased out of the mirror. Seven of nine.

screen: `DAY 1623 COUNTS.` → `BODY, ILLNESS AND AGE · 7 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: AN OLD MONK TOLD TO EASE UP.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often point to the 'divine messengers' (old age, sickness and death) as reminders to practice; some Buddhists reflect daily that they too are subject to ageing.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 83 (Makhadeva Sutta: the king asks his barber to report gray hairs; gives him a village; tells his eldest son the divine messengers have appeared; goes forth; asks that the custom be continued)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.36 (Devaduta Sutta: the divine messengers, an old person, a sick person, a dead person)

sources.quoted: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

notes: Wisdom shape with the unity thread: shared (the passing of days as a teacher, turned toward wisdom) and one honest difference (the psalm asks God to teach; in the sutta the gray hair is the messenger and the king answers by going forth). No ranking. Psalm 90 quoted from the KJV; a Jewish reader may prefer JPS 1917 ('So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom'): confirm and choose.

MN 83 paraphrased: the vast spans of years in the sutta are left out under the claims rule; 'years later' stands in. Confirm the plucked hair placed in the king's palm, the village for the barber, and the custom handed to the eldest son.

AN 3.36 lists five messengers in full (a newborn, an old person, a sick person, a criminal punished, a dead person); the lesson names three as the commonly taught set. Confirm phrasing 'names these messengers' doesn't imply only three.
